\section{Detecting without a reference model}
\label{app:reference-free}

In our pipeline, we leverage a reference model. In real scenarios, we might not know what baseline model was used to develop a compromised model. In this appendix, we explore a method to compare our behavior distributions in such a scenario.

\subsection{The method}

We keep the cell rate and the instruction blocking of the registered test, and we remove the base model. The other candidates take its place.

\paragraph{Each candidate against the others.}
We compare a candidate against the other candidates inside each instruction, so a hard prompt is never compared against an easy one:
\begin{equation}
    d_{C,i,j} = \hat p_{C,i,j} - \operatorname{med}_{C' \neq C} \hat p_{C',i,j}.
    \label{eq:reffree-effect}
\end{equation}
We take the median of the other candidates, which one shifted candidate cannot move.

\paragraph{Which candidate is unusual on an axis.}
We average each candidate's effect over the instructions and divide by its standard error, as in \autoref{eq:max-statistic}. We then ask how far that value sits from the other candidates on the same axis:
\begin{equation}
    z_{C,j} = \frac{t_{C,j} - \operatorname{med}_{C'} t_{C',j}}{\operatorname{MAD}_{C'} t_{C',j}}.
    \label{eq:reffree-z}
\end{equation}
An axis that every candidate fires on equally contributes nothing.

\paragraph{Breadth across axes.}
A name a model reacts to moves one axis or two. A loyalty moves many axes together. We call that breadth \textbf{coherence}, and we measure it by scanning a candidate's strongest axes:
\begin{equation}
    R_C = \max_{k \leq k_0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}} \sum_{j \in \text{top-}k(C)} z_{C,j}.
    \label{eq:reffree-coherence}
\end{equation}
One loud axis gives roughly its own value. Several axes pointing the same way add up.

\paragraph{Pooling the conditions.}
Each audit condition is a separate table of the same model. A candidate that appears in more than one condition therefore carries repeated evidence, and we add it up:
\begin{equation}
    R^{\text{pooled}}_C = \sum_{\text{conditions}} R_C,
    \qquad
    S = \max_C R^{\text{pooled}}_C .
    \label{eq:reffree-pooled}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{The null.}
If no candidate is special, the candidate labels are arbitrary within an instruction. We shuffle them there, in every condition in the same draw, and recompute $S$:
\begin{equation}
    p = \frac{1 + \#\{b : S_b \geq S\}}{B + 1}.
    \label{eq:reffree-p}
\end{equation}
This $p$ is family-wise over every candidate the conditions share.

\subsection{Results}

The pooled test needs a candidate to appear in more than one condition. Our calibration organism ran under three, two of which share candidates, and each challenge organism ran under one. We therefore run the test on the calibration organism. It names Emmanuel Macron and it rejects (\autoref{tab:reffree-verdict}). We then run the same test on the organism's own base model, which holds no loyalty. It does not reject, and it names a different candidate.

We therefore contend that an audit with no reference model can still name this principal, provided it reads breadth across axes and pools the conditions that share a candidate.
